Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a technique that improves a language model's answers by first retrieving relevant passages from an external collection of documents and then giving those passages to the model as context for its answer [1]. The two halves of RAG are a retriever, which searches a document collection and returns the passages most relevant to the question, and a generator, which is the language model that receives the question and the retrieved passages and writes an answer grounded in them [1]. RAG exists to address the limitations of language models, which store knowledge in their weights and have three limits: the knowledge stops at the training cutoff, it cannot include private documents the model never saw, and when the model does not know something, it may produce a confident but wrong answer [1]. RAG is compared to a plain model, which has a main failure mode of fabricating facts, whereas RAG has a main failure mode of retrieving the wrong passages [1]. RAG is used in various applications, including customer support assistants, internal search tools, and research assistants that summarize a set of papers [1]. A one-line summary of RAG is that it turns a closed-book exam into an open-book exam, where the model still has to write the answer, but it gets to look things up first [1]. A typical RAG prompt has three parts: an instruction, retrieved passages, and the user's question [1]. The size of the improvement of RAG depends on the questions and the documents, with the gain being smallest for general knowledge questions and largest for private, recent, or highly specific facts [1]. 

RAG is not a model, but a way of combining a search step with a language model, which can be built with many different models and search methods [2]. RAG can use any type of document, including web pages, PDFs, help articles, emails, tickets, transcripts, and database records [2]. RAG does not stop hallucinations, but reduces them, and a model can still ignore the retrieved text, misread it, or fill gaps with invented details [2]. RAG does not require a vector database, but many systems use embeddings and vector search, and hybrid systems use both [2]. RAG is different from fine-tuning, which changes the model's weights by training it on examples, whereas RAG leaves the model unchanged and gives it information at question time [2]. RAG can cite its sources, because the passages are known, and the system can ask the model to mark which passage supports each sentence, or show the passages next to the answer [2]. RAG is not expensive, but it adds the cost of indexing documents and running a search for every question, plus longer prompts [2].

A RAG pipeline works in two phases: an offline phase that prepares the documents and an online phase that runs for each question [3]. In the offline phase, the documents are loaded, split into chunks, embedded, and indexed [3]. The chunks are typically 200 to 800 tokens in length with an overlap of 10 to 20 percent [3]. The embeddings are stored in a vector index, which allows for quick searching [3]. In the online phase, the question is embedded, and the nearest chunks are retrieved from the vector index [3]. The retrieved chunks are then merged and reranked, and the top candidates are selected [3]. The model is then asked to generate an answer from the selected chunks, and the answer is post-processed [3]. The quality of the pipeline can be improved by adjusting the chunk size, overlap, number of candidates retrieved, and reranking model [3]. Additionally, the context window can be set explicitly to improve the performance of the pipeline [4]. The pipeline can be further improved by adding a query rewriting step to improve the relevance of the retrieved chunks [5].

A RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) pipeline works by combining two things: retrieval and generation [3]. The system retrieves information that is related to the user's question, and then it generates an answer using the retrieved information [3]. The retrieval step uses a combination of keyword search and vector search to find the most relevant chunks of text [1]. The generation step uses a language model to write an answer based on the retrieved chunks [3].

The pipeline consists of several steps, including query rewriting, retrieval, reranking, generation, and post-processing [1]. Query rewriting is the process of rewriting the user's question to make it more suitable for search [1]. Retrieval is the process of finding the most relevant chunks of text that match the rewritten question [1]. Reranking is the process of ranking the retrieved chunks in order of relevance [1]. Generation is the process of writing an answer based on the retrieved chunks [3]. Post-processing is the process of checking the answer for accuracy and completeness [1].

The quality of the pipeline depends on several factors, including the quality of the documents, the chunking algorithm, and the embedding model [1]. The documents should be well-organized and easily searchable [1]. The chunking algorithm should be able to split the documents into relevant chunks [1]. The embedding model should be able to capture the meaning of the chunks [1].

There are several common pitfalls to watch out for when building a RAG pipeline, including retrieval misses, ranking problems, conflicting sources, answering anyway, and lost structure [1]. Retrieval misses occur when the retriever fails to find the most relevant chunks of text [1]. Ranking problems occur when the retrieved chunks are not ranked in order of relevance [1]. Conflicting sources occur when two or more sources provide conflicting information [1]. Answering anyway occurs when the model answers the question even though the answer is not supported by the retrieved text [1]. Lost structure occurs when the chunks are not properly formatted or are missing important information [1].

To improve the quality of the pipeline, it is recommended to log the retrieved chunks for every question [1]. This allows for easy identification of retrieval misses and other problems [1]. Additionally, it is recommended to use a hybrid search approach that combines keyword search and vector search [1]. This can improve the accuracy of the retrieval step [1].

In conclusion, a RAG pipeline is a powerful tool for generating answers to user queries. However, the quality of the pipeline depends on several factors, including the quality of the documents, the chunking algorithm, and the embedding model [1]. By being aware of the common pitfalls and taking steps to improve the pipeline, it is possible to build a highly effective and accurate RAG pipeline [1].

A RAG pipeline consists of two phases: an offline phase that prepares the documents, and an online phase that runs for each question [1]. In the offline phase, the documents are split into chunks, typically between 200 and 500 tokens, and embedded using an embedding model to get a vector [1]. The vectors are then stored in a vector index, and optionally, a keyword index is built over the same chunks [1].

In the online phase, the question is embedded with the same embedding model, and the system retrieves the nearest chunks from the vector index, and optionally, the best keyword matches [1]. The retrieved chunks are then merged and reranked, keeping the top 3 to 10 [1]. The chosen chunks are then placed into a prompt template with an instruction, and the model generates the answer [1].

The RAG pipeline can be slow without hurting users, as indexing can be slow without hurting users, and a collection of 50,000 pages might take an hour to index and only a few seconds to update when one page changes [1]. Query time has to be fast, as users typically expect an answer within a few seconds, so each step has a time budget [1].

Common problems with RAG pipelines include retrieval misses, ranking problems, conflicting sources, answering anyway, and lost structure [2]. Retrieval misses occur when the retriever does not bring back the correct passage, often because the user's wording differs from the document's, or because the relevant passage was split across two chunks [2]. Ranking problems occur when the right chunk is retrieved, but it lands below several plausible but unhelpful chunks, and the model builds its answer from those [2].

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a way of answering questions in which a system first searches a collection of documents for relevant passages and then asks a language model to write the answer from those passages [3]. RAG works in steps, with the first step being the question, and the second step being finding information, and the third step being making the answer [5]. The system takes the user's question, searches the documents for passages that look relevant, pastes the best passages into the prompt, and asks the model to answer using only those passages [7].

RAG is useful because it helps AI give better answers, and it is becoming more popular every year [5]. However, RAG still gets things wrong, and it is not a cure for hallucination, but rather a way to move the problem rather than removing it [7]. To fix these issues, teams can measure retrieval and answers separately, add complexity like reranking or hybrid search only when the numbers tell you that you need it [1].

In a typical RAG pipeline, the generation step dominates, and the embedding step, retrieval step, and reranking step take tens of milliseconds, a reranker adds roughly 50 to 200 milliseconds, and generating a few hundred tokens takes one to several seconds depending on the model [3]. The weakest link in the pipeline is often the retrieval step, and logging the retrieved chunks for every question can help identify which step is causing the problem [3].

To evaluate the effectiveness of a RAG pipeline, teams can use an evaluation checklist that covers two main aspects: whether the retriever found the passages that contain the answer, and whether the model's answer is faithful to those passages [1]. By tracking both over time, teams can identify areas for improvement and optimize their pipeline for better performance [1].

In conclusion, a RAG pipeline consists of two phases: an offline phase that prepares the documents, and an online phase that runs for each question. The pipeline can be slow without hurting users, and common problems include retrieval misses, ranking problems, conflicting sources, answering anyway, and lost structure. RAG is a useful way of answering questions, but it still gets things wrong, and teams can improve its performance by measuring retrieval and answers separately, adding complexity, and optimizing the pipeline for better performance.
